correctness.rationale: The theorem is correct. Any \(m\) separating formulas assign an \(m\)-bit truth vector to each quotient class, so \(k\le2^m\). Conversely, label the \(k\) classes injectively by \(m=\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) bit strings and define each bit coordinate by the union of all classes carrying bit one; finite CPC defines every such union. Equality of truth vectors is then exactly the coequivalence. The Bell/Stirling census follows from the bijection with partitions of the \(2^n\) valuations. The bundled checker exhausts \(n\le3\), but the proof is uniform and elementary.

originality.rationale: Originality fails under the implication standard. The full primary source's Example 3.10 already identifies every CPC coequivalence with an equivalence relation on the finite valuation set and proves separation by taking a definable class-indicator formula for each quotient class. In CPC every union of classes is definable. Replacing one-hot class indicators by the ordinary binary code of the \(k\) classes gives \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) coordinates, and the matching pigeonhole lower bound is the elementary fact that \(m\) Boolean coordinates distinguish at most \(2^m\) classes. The Bell/Stirling census is the standard enumeration of partitions of a finite set. Thus the final theorem is mechanically implied by the inspected source plus textbook finite coding/counting facts even though the exact optimization is not written there.
